title: The Philippine Immigration Detention Center: If You Don't Pay, Your Deportation Never Moves
dek: A Chinese surfer was locked up in the Philippines for 41 days. What he saw wasn't a prison — it was a business with a price list: beds, boxed meals, phones, lawyer fees, every one of them bought with cash. Those who don't pay stay locked up for years, even decades.
why: StoryFM's Behind Bars series. Medium information density but solid detail. The first half is a personal ordeal; the second half — the gang economy inside the detention center, the ransom quotes from scam companies, the lawyers jacking up prices on the spot — is the part actually worth your time.
who: Founders and going-global practitioners interested in the situation of overseas Chinese, the Philippine business environment, and the gray-industry and immigration-corruption machinery.
skip: 6:29-9:14 — the surfing career and startup background, unrelated to the core mechanism.

points.h: The Immigration Bureau quoted 1.5 million pesos to walk free on the spot
points.body: The night Feili was arrested, Immigration Bureau people pulled him aside and quietly said, "I can help you." After the lawyer communicated, the feedback came back: give 1.5 million pesos, about 160,000-170,000 RMB, and you can be released immediately, no problem at all. Of the 12 to 13 people arrested in the same batch, no one agreed to pay. Everyone thought it was impossible that such a thing could still exist in 2026, and wanted to resolve it through normal legal procedures. But the price of refusing was this: they were transferred from the holding cell at the General City police station to the Immigration Bureau's main detention center in Manila, where Feili ultimately spent 41 days.

points.h: When his phone was confiscated, the money in Gcash was transferred out
points.body: When Feili was detained his phone was taken, and they asked for his unlock code. He assumed it was normal procedure and gave it. His phone unlock code was the same as his Gcash payment password — the Philippine equivalent of Alipay. For the next four or five days, no matter how he applied, he couldn't get the phone back, until he kept pressuring the Chinese consulate and the lawyer, and the phone was finally returned. When he turned it on, the interface had all switched to English, and the Gcash transfer records showed money had been sent out — but the night before he got the phone back, it had been transferred back in. There was only about 1,000 RMB in there. Feili said it wasn't about the amount; it was that while the phone wasn't in his hands, someone had touched it. He reasoned that many Chinese doing gray-industry scams in Manila who get arrested go through this same layer of fleecing, but they don't dare go to the Chinese consulate, because their phones contain a mass of criminal evidence.

points.h: The air conditioning and takeout the Immigration Bureau promised were just another form
points.body: For those unwilling to buy their own plane ticket to transfer, the Immigration Bureau would take turns working on them, saying the Manila Immigration Bureau had great conditions, air conditioning, lots of freedom, you could work out, play basketball, order takeout, use your phone. Feili said they weren't lying — there really was air conditioning, you really could order takeout, it was just another form, a completely different form. Arriving at the main detention center was around 3 a.m. After getting off the vehicle, what he saw was a square area, an outer layer of iron grating, a sheet-metal roof above, iron cages like dog kennels all around, and inside, communal sleeping platforms, several hundred people. At 3 a.m. many people weren't sleeping — bare-chested, wearing just underwear, clinging to the iron cages to stare at the newcomers. Feili said he and the other foreigners didn't say a word for several minutes after getting off, then it hit them: they'd been lied to by the Immigration Bureau.

points.h: The detention center is a business invested in by a Chinese boss
points.body: What Feili heard inside was that this Immigration Bureau detention center was invested in by a Chinese boss, in cooperation with the Immigration Bureau, and that the beds, toilets and other facilities were all newly built by the Chinese boss. Foreigners could just stay, but Chinese coming in had to pay. The lowest-tier communal platform bed was 10,000 pesos a month, about 1,100-1,200 RMB. Wealthy pan zong and gambling bosses could pay 50,000 pesos a month, about 6,000-plus RMB, for a so-called "air-conditioned room" — actually the same bed, just wrapped in tin foil and wooden boards, with a foam box of ice beside it, a hole cut in the box, and an exhaust fan drawing the cold air into the bed. That's where the Immigration Bureau's original claim of "there's air conditioning inside" came from.

points.h: Chinese gangs collect protection money: you want out without paying?
points.body: On Feili's first day inside, the head of the Chinese gang came to him to collect the "rumor fee," saying the facilities inside were all their investment, it couldn't possibly be free to stay. Feili said he had no money, he was here to serve time, how could he have to pay on top of that. The gang boss said in a threatening tone: you're already in here and don't want to spend money, and you still think you're getting out? Feili learned that the place is run by gangs, and the Chinese gang monopolizes all the food, clothing and daily life of the Chinese, running a Chinese restaurant and a Chinese supermarket. The whole detention center held about 200 people; when Feili went in it was the off-season, and there were still over 100 Chinese, more than half of them gambling and gray industry. The Chinese gang's employees drew wages — the head chef 10,000 pesos a month, the assistant cook 5,000 pesos — very low wages, but many people couldn't get out precisely because they had no money for a lawyer, so they could only work to earn.

points.h: A Yunnan man held for over a year; his family thought he'd died in Southeast Asia
points.body: A man from Yunnan asked Feili for help. Before the pandemic he'd been lured to the Philippines by a high-salary recruitment ad; the moment he landed his phone and passport were taken, and he was dragged into a compound to do telecom fraud. With poor performance he was shocked with an electric baton by his supervisor every day. After the company was busted he served a few months, then was transferred to the Immigration Bureau detention center. The normal deportation procedure is simple — a few departments sign off, you buy your own plane ticket, and you can go — but the Immigration Bureau, in order to extract money, keeps you locked up for a very long time; without paying, the procedure doesn't move. He'd already been held for over a year, with not a cent, no phone, eating only prison food every day, unable to reach his family, who thought he'd died in Southeast Asia. Feili helped him write a letter in Chinese, translated it into English, and through a Japanese man's introduction got to see the warden. The warden had a guard bring Feili's phone, and had Xiaopang add his father on WeChat and send a selfie and a voice message. Afterwards the Immigration Bureau bought a feature phone specifically to solve this problem.

points.h: Scam company ransom: 3 million pesos per person
points.body: The only Chinese person Feili talked with much came from a scam company. The company's 70 or 80 people were surrounded by the Immigration Bureau together with the police and the NBI — three departments. The first wave of fleecing was the NBI and police locking each person in a toilet, because there are no cameras in the toilets, and taking everything valuable off them. The second wave was the Immigration Bureau negotiating ransom with the company boss — the quote differed per person, 1 million, 2 million, 3 million pesos, depending on the person in charge's mood. That company negotiated at 3 million pesos per person, about 300,000-plus RMB. The boss ultimately ransomed 30 people, exactly the 30 held on one floor; the rest were promised food deliveries until they got out. This young man ran an operation targeting the Japanese market, scamming middle-aged Japanese women; in his best month he made 2 million RMB, and bought a house and a car in his small hometown county. Later he was kidnapped by a friend, several hundred thousand was transferred out of his accounts, and a corrupt cop pinned an illegal gun-possession charge on him, so he couldn't leave.

points.h: The Philippine lawyer raised his price on the spot when he saw he was Chinese
points.body: In Cebu, through a Lithuanian's introduction, Feili met a Philippine lawyer who quoted 200,000 pesos, about 20,000-plus RMB, done in four weeks. After arriving in Manila the lawyer came to visit, saw he was Chinese, and immediately raised the price, saying that was the old price, the new price required another 120,000 pesos, about 10,000-plus RMB. Feili decided not to use him, and gave up the deposit, turning instead to a Chinese intermediary. The Chinese intermediary quoted 30,000-plus RMB, four to six weeks, no more than six weeks. Feili said the truly reliable Chinese intermediaries know this procedure inside out, because everyone locked up in there is Chinese. In the end he was held inside for over 30 days, plus Cebu, 41 days total. The Lithuanian who introduced the Philippine lawyer still hadn't gotten out when Feili sent him a message.

But it's not about the amount of money — while the phone wasn't in my hands, it was transferred out.

Look at his corrupt bureaucratic system and its people as separate things. I still believe Filipinos are fundamentally very good people, but the bureaucratic system is truly too corrupt — and it's the kind that drinks blood, human blood.
